findings.title: Failed messages are still marked complete and committed, giving at-most-once semantics
findings.body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, exceptions from result_processor are caught and only logged (line 144-147), and the finally block at line 149 always calls offset_tracker.complete_offset. The offset is then treated as processed and will be committed by the commit loop. Combined with ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py line 53-54) which also swallows all exceptions, any transient failure (e.g. a DB error while handling a result) silently drops the message and advances the committed offset past it, so the message is never retried. This contradicts the class docstring's guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns the consumer into an at-most-once pipeline with silent data loss.

findings.title: close() permanently kills the shared queue pool, breaking rebalance recovery
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets the shutdown flag on every worker, shuts down every queue.Queue, and joins the threads. The queue_pool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies. Arroyo closes the current strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on partition rebalance/reassignment (e.g. when partitions are revoked and later reassigned, or when running multiple strategies per process). After the first close(), all worker threads have exited, but the factory keeps the same (now dead) pool and creates a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy on top of it. All subsequently submitted items pile up in the dead queues with nothing consuming them: no processing, no offset commits, unbounded memory growth, and the consumer stalls. close() should only stop the strategy's commit thread and drain, leaving pool lifecycle to the factory.

findings.title: Uses queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown which only exist on Python 3.13+
findings.body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker.run catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132, 142). Queue.shutdown and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On any older supported interpreter, importing is fine but calling shutdown() raises AttributeError (caught and logged at line 239-240, leaving workers blocked forever on q.get()) and the except clause referencing queue.ShutDown raises AttributeError inside run, killing the worker thread. Verify the project's minimum Python version or use a sentinel-based shutdown.

findings.title: Docstring claims backpressure but queues are unbounded
findings.body: The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' (and FixedQueuePool has no maxsize), but each queue.Queue is created with no maxsize (line 185), and submit() never blocks. The arroyo consumer can therefore poll and enqueue messages far faster than workers process them, with the only limit being process memory. Under a slow-consumer backlog this leads to unbounded memory growth and, since processing lags arbitrarily behind, offsets are held back indefinitely while messages accumulate. Either give queues a maxsize so submit blocks, or remove the backpressure claim and add a depth-based guard/metric alert.

findings.title: Background commit thread commits without regard to partition ownership
findings.body: The commit loop runs every second and calls commit_function(committable) for all partitions ever seen by the OffsetTracker, including partitions that may have been revoked during a rebalance. Committing offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns violates Kafka consumer-group protocol (the commit is rejected or, worse, races with the new owner). There is no cancellation of in-flight work or clearing of tracker state on partition revocation, and commit also proceeds concurrently with close()/terminate(): shutdown_event is set, but the loop can already be past the wait(1.0) and issue a commit while the pool is shutting down. The strategy needs to stop committing for revoked partitions (e.g. filter against currently assigned partitions passed to create_with_partitions) and re-check shutdown_event before committing.

findings.title: --max-workers help text/semantics conflate worker threads and queue count
findings.body: In thread-queue-parallel mode, max_workers sets num_queues (the number of queues, each with one worker thread), and the default when max_workers is None is 20 — whereas in batched-parallel mode the default is ThreadPoolExecutor's default. The shared click option's help ('The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode') hides that for this mode the value also caps per-key parallelism at exactly one thread per queue and that a deploy changing max_workers remaps every group to a different queue (hash(group_key) % num_queues), which can momentarily reorder processing relative to items still in old queues. Consider documenting the remapping caveat and the differing default.
